hypothesis: Bead on the FINE fold levels + hexagon on the COARSE ones reads more clearly than bead everywhere (HANDOFF §8 variant 2), and is cheaper (§9)
split_knob: knob_162 = SPLIT_AT, an ld cut; settled on 0.5 (bead on i=7,8,9; hex on i=4,5,6). Probed 0.3/0.5/0.7 in journals/lab/shots/split-probe-sheet.png
fine_end_of_i: HIGH i = FINE. scale *= s (s~2) every iteration so the fold domain shrinks as i grows; corroborated by the level-window comment (gDepthFocus 0 -> 'coarse levels dominate' weights 1-ld, and ld=(i-FIRST)/(LEVELS-1-FIRST) so ld=0 at i=FIRST=4).
why: Motif recognisability is set by ON-SCREEN CELL SIZE, and the coarse levels are the only ones whose cells are large enough for a silhouette to be nameable. Putting hex on the coarse levels reserves every large cell for the hexagon and leaves the bead only at scales a few pixels across, where it degrades from a motif into speckle texture. The split therefore reads as the ORIGINAL hex lattice with a dirty warm texture overlay - busier, not clearer. Monotone across the probe: as more coarse levels revert to hex (SPLIT_AT 0.3 -> 0.7) the bead gets less nameable, and all-bead is the only arm with coherent non-hexagonal closed contours. This also answers the coordinator's boundary-crossings note: the split removes bead exactly from the levels where radial boundary crossings are most visible, so it HURTS legibility rather than helping it.
perf: IN-APP FPS IS USELESS HERE - vsync-capped at 144Hz on an RTX 4090 and the app has a dynamic resolution scaler: all-hex 130.1, all-bead 137.9, split 140.8 fps (mean of 3, 1000x800), ordering is scheduling noise. Real cost measured offscreen at 2048x2048, median ms/frame: all-hex 0.473 / all-bead 0.453 / split 0.460 - IDENTICAL. Mechanism: GLSL mix() evaluates both operands, so beadDist() and all 6 dependent texture fetches run in EVERY arm including all-hex; step() gates the mix weight, not the fetch. §9's saving is not realised by a per-level mix at all. Converting the mix to a uniform branch that actually skips the sample (split-branch.frag) does show a gradient: all-hex ~0.37, split ~0.38-0.43, all-bead ~0.45-0.50 ms - i.e. the entire 6-fetch bead cost is only ~0.08-0.11ms of ~0.46ms (~20%), so halving it buys ~10% of frame cost on desktop. NOT a mobile rescue on its own; @mobile: true was NOT copied into any header and mobile remains unmeasured.
darkening: Did not reproduce, and the split does the OPPOSITE. Mean luminance, t=8, n=3 at 1000x800: all-hex 13.04 (12.04-14.17, ~+/-8% run-to-run noise from lattice-nav frame-count state), all-bead 14.29 (14.12-14.42), split 17.54 (16.68-18.42). So all-bead is +10% BRIGHTER than hex for mon-kiku (matches the tomoe teammate), and the split is +35% brighter than hex / +23% brighter than all-bead - well outside the noise band. Cause: the split overlaps two cell families whose coverage does not coincide (coarse hex rings + fine bead blobs), so lit area ADDS. A counter-ratchet was built and MEASURED, then removed: scaling the line-coverage term f by 0.74 moved mean luminance only -2.6% (17.54 -> 17.09), so the intensity path saturates and coverage scaling is the wrong lever - the compensation has to go on the lum/lightness path instead. Shipped file is therefore the clean single-variable arm.
next: Test the REVERSE split - bead on COARSE levels, hex on FINE. The mechanism predicts it is both the most legible (bead keeps the only cells big enough to name) and genuinely the cheapest (2-3 fetches, and they are on the coarse levels), which would make it the real §9 mitigation rather than variant 2.
